title: Haf's Whispering Weather Vane
markdown:
Breezy Hollow hummed with quiet joy, and Haf was its gentle heart. His workshop smelled of wood shavings and warm metal, a place where creaky gates and little rooftop birds learned to spin again. His fingers danced, coaxing paint and tin into life.

He was a watcher too. The wind blew the same for everyone, and somehow each friend heard a different song.

Poppy the squirrel, a furry blur with a bouncy tail, would twitch her nose. "The wind's shouting for nuts!" And zoom.

Jun the mole, who loved the quiet earth, would peek out. "A brisk breeze. A good day to check tunnels. The wind whispers a warning."

Even Mrs. Higgins, whose bakery smelled of cinnamon hugs, would smile. "That breeze tickles my dough. It tells me I need more yeast for fluffy buns."

Haf found this endlessly curious. One sigh of air. Three messages. He wanted everyone to see that the whispers were cousins, not arguments. An idea, a rather lovely one, began to brew among the shavings.

Tap-tap-tap went his hammer. Scrape-scrape went his file. This was not ordinary mending. He found a sturdy pole and attached several little pointers. One leaping squirrel, ready for adventure. One digging mole, sleek and determined. One soft fluffy cloud. He painted them bright: sunny orange for Poppy, earthy brown for Jun, dreamy white for the cloud — and, privately, for buns. The Breezy Hollow Festival was a week away.

Festival day dawned bright and honestly breezy. Haf carried the vane to the village green. Poppy was mid-leap. Jun was sniffing clover.

"Friends," Haf called, calm and clear. "I made something for us."

Poppy scampered. "Ooh, shiny! Does it point to the biggest nuts?"

Jun shuffled near. "Will it tell us if the sky might cry?"

Haf chuckled. "Something even better." He pushed the pole into the grass. A puff swished by. The orange squirrel spun toward the woods. The brown mole dipped toward the earth. The white cloud twirled, in no hurry at all.

"Look. Same wind. The squirrel leans toward Poppy's errands. The mole leans toward Jun's tunnels. The cloud is simply enjoying itself — and possibly thinking of Mrs. Higgins's buns."

Poppy blinked, then grinned. "So it is telling me to explore. I knew it."

Jun's rumble held a new softness. "And I should check the tunnels. Just to be sure."

Haf beamed. "The wind is only the wind. What we make of the whisper — that's ours. The vane doesn't choose a winner. It lets all three stories spin on one pole."

They looked at the pointers, then at each other, then at the sky. Giggles bubbled. Jun sighed, content.

"Haf, that's brilliant!" called Mrs. Higgins, flour on her apron like a weather report of her own.

The vane stood tall and cheerful. The wind went on being itself. Haf, quiet craftsman, felt warmth spread through him — not because he had given a speech, but because Poppy and Jun had watched the same gust and not argued about it.

He wondered, wiping orange paint from his thumb, whether tomorrow's wind would send the squirrel pointer toward the bakery instead, and whether Poppy would still hear nuts, or cinnamon, and whether that would count as the same message in a new hat.
